page2_img_1.png.title: Simplified contemporary code review workflow
page2_img_1.png.description: A six-step schematic showing how an author, a review tool, a reviewer, and the code repository interact in contemporary (tool-based) code review. The author submits a patch-set and description to the code-review infrastructure, which (step 3) notifies the reviewer; the reviewer inspects the changes (the figure implies side‑by‑side diffs and inline comments) and either (step 4) requests changes back to the author or (step 5) approves the change. The author then uploads revised patch-sets as needed and, after approval, (step 6) checks the code into the repository — illustrating the iterative, asynchronous cycle supported by tools such as Gerrit, Phabricator, or ReviewBoard.

page10_img_2.png.title: Reasons author identity matters when accepting review requests
page10_img_2.png.description: Horizontal bar chart (Fig. 4) lists five reasons reviewers reported the author’s identity mattered: Reputation, Relationship, Time and effort, Areas of expertise, and Other. Reputation is the top reason for both groups (roughly ~60% of OSS respondents and slightly lower for Microsoft), while OSS respondents emphasize Relationship much more than Microsoft (OSS ≈45% vs Microsoft ≈25%). Microsoft respondents more often cite technical/practical factors — Time and effort and Areas of expertise — than OSS respondents (Time/effort ≈35–40% for Microsoft vs ≈25% for OSS; Areas of expertise ≈20–25% for Microsoft vs ≈15% for OSS), with ‘Other’ being rare for both.

page7_img_2.png.title: Survey respondents’ primary projects (OSS vs Microsoft)
page7_img_2.png.description: A two-column listing of the specific Open Source and Microsoft projects named by survey respondents, with the number in parentheses indicating how many respondents reported that project as their primary project. The OSS column is led by Qt (36), OpenStack (32), CyanogenMod (28), Android (19), Linux kernel (16), and Chromium OS (14), with many smaller projects and an "Others" group (24). The Microsoft column is dominated by large product teams—Bing (54), Windows (48), Office (43), Azure (24), Visual Studio (22), etc.—and also includes a large "Others" bucket (131) representing many additional Microsoft teams.

page7_img_1.png.title: Cronbach’s alpha for peer-impression constructs (OSS vs Microsoft)
page7_img_1.png.description: The table reports Cronbach’s alpha for four behavioral constructs (Trust, Perception of Expertise, Reliability, Friendship) measured separately in the OSS and Microsoft surveys, with an interpretation label for each value. OSS: Trust = .756 (Acceptable), Perception of Expertise = .811 (Good), Reliability = .810 (Good), Friendship = .700 (Acceptable). Microsoft: Trust = .798 (Acceptable), Perception of Expertise = .839 (Good), Reliability = .736 (Acceptable), Friendship = .758 (Acceptable). These results indicate acceptable-to-good internal consistency for the scales (per conventional thresholds), supporting the authors’ use of these measures to analyze code-review-related peer impressions.

page21_img_1.png.title: Grayscale author headshot portrait in office setting
page21_img_1.png.description: A black-and-white head-and-shoulders portrait of a young adult male facing the camera with a neutral expression and a slight smile. He has short hair, a trimmed beard/chinstrap, and is wearing a collared shirt; the background shows office cubicle panels and overhead lighting, indicating an indoor workplace. The image is presented as an author portrait headshot in the paper’s biographical section.

page5_img_table_1.png.title: Behavioral scale items for peer-impression constructs
page5_img_table_1.png.description: A tabular list of the behavioral-scale statements used to measure four peer-impression constructs (Trust, Perception of Expertise, Reliability, and Friendship). For each construct the table shows item identifiers (e.g., trust_1..trust_5, expertise_1..expertise_5, reliability_1..reliability_5, friendship_1..friendship_6) and the exact statement respondents evaluated (examples: trust_1 “My communication with him/her is more informal,” expertise_1 “It is easier for me to identify whether s/he has the ability to provide help in a specific project area,” reliability_1 “I am more comfortable assigning a critical task to him or her,” friendship_1 “I would feel a stronger sense of loss at his/her departure from the project”). Two rightmost columns mark which items were included in the OSS and Microsoft surveys; a footnote indicates items marked with an asterisk were dropped during analysis to improve internal consistency. The table served as the basis for the 7-point comparison scale used to assess how code-review partners differ from non-code-review partners in the study.

page20_img_3.png.title: Black-and-white smiling male headshot portrait
page20_img_3.png.description: A tightly cropped grayscale head-and-shoulders photograph of a smiling man, showing his face turned slightly toward the camera with teeth visible. He wears a dark collared shirt and is positioned against a textured brick-wall background; the crop emphasizes his face and upper torso. The image is presented as an author biography portrait in the paper (page 20), adjacent to the biographical text.

page13_img_1.png.title: Impact of high-quality code on peer perceptions (OSS vs Microsoft)
page13_img_1.png.description: Horizontal bars compare the percent of OSS (dark bars) and Microsoft (light bars) respondents who said high-quality or outstanding code affected their view of the author across four aspects. About 60% of OSS respondents (vs ~36% of Microsoft respondents) reported it improved impressions of the author’s personal characteristics; roughly 37% of OSS (vs ~47% Microsoft) said it helped build relationships; and about 36% of OSS (vs ~48% Microsoft) said it encouraged future collaboration. The chart shows OSS developers emphasize personal-characteristic impressions from good code, whereas Microsoft developers emphasize relationship- and collaboration-building effects; the “Other” category is minimal for both groups.

page8_img_1.png.title: Why developers consider code review important (OSS vs Microsoft)
page8_img_1.png.description: Horizontal grouped bar chart (Fig. 2) comparing Microsoft (light blue) and OSS (dark blue) respondents on reasons they find peer code review important. 'Maintainability' is the top reason for both groups (OSS ≈71%, Microsoft ≈61%), while 'Knowledge sharing' is emphasized much more by Microsoft respondents (around the low‑40% range) than OSS respondents (roughly mid‑20% range). 'Functional defects' is the third most cited reason (Microsoft ≈37% vs OSS ≈28%), with smaller percentages for 'Community building', 'Minor errors/typos', and 'Other'. The paper notes these distributions differ significantly between the surveys (χ² test, p < .001).

page4_img_1.png.title: Small circular decorative page graphic
page4_img_1.png.description: A small grayscale circular page graphic (ornament/watermark) near the bottom of page 4, appearing as a light circle with subtle concentric shading and no axes, labels, or numeric content. It is a purely decorative element placed between the end of the 'Impact of Code Review on Peer Impressions' text and the start of Section 4 ('Research Method' / 'Participant Selection'), and does not convey study data or findings. The surrounding page text lists the four behavioral constructs (trustworthiness, reliability, perception of expertise, friendship), but the graphic itself is unrelated to those scale items and serves only as a page graphic.

page10_img_1.png.title: Median weekly hours in code review by experience (OSS vs Microsoft)
page10_img_1.png.description: Vertical bar chart shows median hours per week spent in code reviews for four experience groups (Low, Medium, High, Veteran) separately for OSS and Microsoft respondents. For both OSS and Microsoft the median time increases with developer experience, and OSS developers consistently spend more time reviewing than Microsoft developers (overall medians reported in the paper: OSS = 5 hrs/week, Microsoft = 4 hrs/week). The authors report these differences across experience groups are statistically significant (Kruskal–Wallis: OSS χ2 = 8.16, p = 0.043; Microsoft χ2 = 8.43, p = 0.038) and note that paid OSS contributors review more (median 5 hrs) than volunteer OSS participants (median 3 hrs).

page20_img_2.png.title: Grayscale portrait headshot of a male author in suit and tie
page20_img_2.png.description: A cropped black-and-white headshot showing a middle‑aged man from the chest up against a dark background; he is smiling, has short hair, and wears a jacket, white shirt, and patterned tie. The photo is positioned next to an author biographical blurb in the paper; the adjacent text reports a Ph.D. (University of Maryland, 2003), an academic appointment as an associate professor, and research interests including empirical software engineering, peer code review, human factors, and software quality. The image functions as an author portrait accompanying that biography rather than as a figure presenting study data.

page16_img_1.png.title: Perception-of-expertise rating distributions for code-review partners (OSS vs Microsoft)
page16_img_1.png.description: Two horizontal panel bar charts (top = OSS, bottom = Microsoft) show the distribution of responses for four perception-of-expertise scale items (legend: expertise_1 … expertise_4) across a recoded seven-point scale from “Non code review partner” (left) through “Both” (center) to “Code review partner” (right). For both OSS and Microsoft panels the bars are heavily concentrated on the positive side (labels 1, 2, and “Code review partner”), indicating that roughly 70–80% of respondents reported better perceptions of expertise for their code-review partners than for non-review partners. Very few respondents selected the negative end of the scale, and the overall pattern is similar between OSS and Microsoft, with each expertise item following the same positive skew. Conveys that code-review interactions are associated with substantially higher perceived expertise of peers in both communities.

page15_img_1.png.title: Impact of Poor-Quality Code on Peer Perceptions (OSS vs Microsoft)
page15_img_1.png.description: Grouped horizontal bar chart (dark blue = OSS, light blue = Microsoft) showing how poorly written code influences reviewers’ impressions across four categories: work habits, inexperience, future collaborations, and other. OSS respondents most often indicated poor code signals bad work habits (≈62%) and suggests inexperience (≈51%), while far fewer OSS respondents said it affected future collaborations (≈27%). Microsoft respondents were less likely to cite work habits (≈38%) or inexperience (≈24%) but far more likely to report that poor code reduced future collaborations (≈62%). The paper notes these differences are statistically significant (χ² = 52.79, p < .001); the “Other” category is comparatively small for both groups (roughly 10–20%).

page12_img_1.png.title: Characteristics indicating poor code (OSS vs Microsoft rankings)
page12_img_1.png.description: A pair of stacked horizontal bar charts (left: OSS, right: Microsoft) shows how developers ranked ten code characteristics by importance for indicating poor code; each bar is segmented by the rank assigned (dark blue = Most important, then progressively lighter colors = 2nd–5th most important) and the x-axis is percent of respondents. For both OSS and Microsoft respondents the top three signals are Poor readability, Unnecessary complexity, and Does not maintain application integrity (largest dark-blue and blue segments), while Lack of comments and A large parameter list to a function are among the least frequently chosen top indicators. The ordering is sorted by the OSS survey ranks, and the plot highlights a notable difference: “Does not follow coding convention” is ranked higher by OSS respondents (4th) than by Microsoft respondents (8th).

page11_img_1.png.title: Factors influencing acceptance of code review requests
page11_img_1.png.description: A two-column page excerpt from the paper showing the qualitative findings about why a reviewer considers the author’s identity when accepting a code review. Visible section headings include “Relationship with the Author,” “Reputation of the Author,” “Area of Expertise,” and “Anticipated Time/Effort to Review,” each followed by multiple participant quotations labeled (e.g., OSS-60, OSS-20, OSS-276, MS-90, MS-325, MS-12, OSS-176, OSS-114). The quotes illustrate the paper’s reported themes: OSS respondents emphasize personal relationships, reciprocity, trust, and reputation when prioritizing reviews, whereas Microsoft respondents emphasize the author’s expertise and the expected time/effort required. A large diagonal “preprint” watermark and section numbering (6.3.4) are also visible on the page.

page20_img_1.png.title: Grayscale author headshot portrait in paper biography
page20_img_1.png.description: A grayscale head-and-shoulders portrait of an adult person wearing a dark jacket and a light collared shirt, facing the camera with a neutral expression. The rectangular photo is cropped on the left side of the page and is adjacent to columns of biographical text; a decorative page graphic partly overlaps the lower right corner. The image is presented as a formal author portrait accompanying the paper’s biography section.

page17_img_1.png.title: Importance of code reviews by Microsoft respondents' site distribution
page17_img_1.png.description: Horizontal bar chart comparing reasons Microsoft developers gave for why code review is important, grouped by three respondent types (most review requests come from a different site, most from the same site, or about half from each). The y-axis lists six reasons (Maintainability; Knowledge sharing; Functional defects; Community building; Minor errors/typos; Other) and the x-axis shows percentage of respondents. Maintainability is the top reason for all three groups (about 60–70% of respondents), followed by knowledge sharing (~40–50%); functional-defect detection is cited less often and varies the most across groups (roughly ~20% to ~50%); community building is a moderate factor (~25–40%); minor errors/typos and Other are cited by the fewest respondents (under ~25% and very small, respectively). Overall the chart shows the same ranking of motivations across collocated, distributed, and mixed-site Microsoft teams with only modest differences in percentages.

page12_img_2.png.title: Reviewer methods to remediate poor code (Microsoft vs OSS)
page12_img_2.png.description: Horizontal bar chart (light blue = Microsoft, dark blue = OSS) comparing how reviewers help poor-quality code: the vast majority in both groups (>80%) add comments in the review tool. Microsoft respondents are much more likely than OSS respondents to use external communications (face‑to‑face, IM/email/Skype) to resolve issues, while OSS respondents are substantially more likely to simply rewrite or fix the code themselves. Mentoring, providing examples, and rejecting until improved are used by smaller but notable proportions in both groups. The paper notes these distributions differ significantly (χ² = 93.29, df = 6, p < .001) and explains the pattern: Microsoft reviewers prefer side channels to speed resolution and mentor authors, whereas OSS reviewers (often volunteers) sometimes edit patches themselves to get changes merged.
